title: Where death is, I am not
hookLine: Epicurus: death is nothing to us, for when we are, death is not (Letter to Menoeceus)

lines: I WAS NOT, I WAS, I AM NOT.
cards: On some old Roman gravestones, archaeologists keep finding the same short line, sometimes just as initials. In Latin it runs: I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care. It sounds bleak at first.
Then strangely calm. Whoever carved it was likely echoing a teaching from the Garden, an argument Epicurus made to his friend Menoeceus about the thing people fear most.
The argument fits in a single sentence, and people are still arguing with it.

teach.h: WHILE WE ARE, DEATH IS NOT.
teach.b: First, the argument. In the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus says: get used to thinking that death is nothing to us. Everything good and bad is a matter of feeling, and death is the end of feeling.
So while we are, death is not here; and when death is here, we are not. It never meets us. Second, the fear it's aimed at.
Epicurus wasn't trying to make dying painless, or losing someone easy.

teach.h: NOT DYING: THE DREAD OF BEING DEAD.
teach.b: He was aiming at a specific dread: the fear of being dead, of some terrible state afterward. If there's no one there to suffer it, he says, there's nothing to fear in it. Third, a later echo.
The Roman poet Lucretius, an Epicurean, added a second picture: think of all the time before you were born. It didn't trouble you. The time after you die, he said, is a mirror of it.
Fourth, honesty about where people stand. Epicurus's argument depends on his belief that the soul is made of atoms and scatters at death.
Many people, in many traditions, believe something continues after death, and find comfort there instead.
Others, especially in the Garden's tradition, find comfort exactly here, in nothing to fear. The path doesn't settle that.
Thoughtful people for two thousand years have found this one sentence steadying, or troubling, or both.
Either way, it asks something useful: is it death you fear, or something about living, like unfinished things, or leaving people behind? Those, at least, can be worked on today.

how: Epicureans have long repeated the teaching that death is nothing to us as a remedy for the fear of being dead, and the Latin epitaph 'I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care' appears on many Roman tombs.

o: a Roman emperor who wrote about dying well
a Roman general who feared death in battle
an Epicurean poet of the mirror before birth

games.q: where death is, I am not. tap the pairs.
p: the time before birth, a mirror
I was not, I was, I am not

s: Epicurus said dying and grief are never painful
he aimed at the fear of being dead, not at pain or loss.
Epicurus's argument rests on his view that death ends all feeling
for him, the soul is made of atoms that scatter at death.
Lucretius compared the time after death to the time before birth
it didn't trouble us then, he said.

games.q: a friend says, "I'm terrified of being dead." what would Epicurus answer?
o: you'll be punished if you're not careful.
when death is here, you aren't, so there's no one to suffer it.
games.why: Epicurus says death never meets us: while we are, it isn't; when it is, we aren't. many people, from many traditions, answer differently.

practice: If this topic is heavy for you today, simply follow the breath instead. If you're willing, hold Epicurus's sentence lightly: while I am, death is not; when death is, I am not.
Don't decide whether you agree; notice what it stirs, then ask quietly what, underneath, you're actually afraid of, and whether it's something you can tend to while you're here.

wordCard.voice: Lucretius. The Epicurean poet who pictured the time after death as a mirror of all the time before you were born. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: death is nothing to us. Epicurus's words, in the Letter to Menoeceus and the second Principal Doctrine.

carryVoice: Your line: where death is, I'm not. Some find it steadying, some don't, and both are welcome here. That's day six hundred fifty-two.
